availability. ESPN also lists Sharks Quentin Musty and Kyle Keyser on IR. Final

Home ice and a better early record support the San Jose side. Askarov has a higher
season save percentage than projected Buffalo starter Ellis. His last two games
show 70 saves on 74 shots per the goalie report; San Jose has scored 16 goals in
its past three games. Buffalo has gone 0-1-2 in its past three. [2,3] Celebrini has
15 points (5 goals) in 10 games in official NHL skater data; he is the main offensive
reason for my Sharks lean. [2]

Countercase: the background books favor Buffalo, whose roster still includes
Thompson and Dahlin. San Jose's defense is also vulnerable: NHL goalie team totals
show a 3.50 GAA versus Buffalo 3.64, while Askarov's season GAA is worse than Ellis's
in a larger but still small sample. The Sharks are missing Wennberg/Chernyshov.
[2,4] Higher save percentage is not a guarantee or an independent probability model.

that the underdog is mispriced.

Art movements of different decades. Tested it with GPT 2.5

Prompt: 4 images: 4:5, stunning art movements of different decades: INPUT: $ SUBJECT

Create ONE tall vertical illustrated poster about $ SUBJECT.

The image must automatically reinterpret $ SUBJECT as a playful,
dense, symbolic character-collage.

────────────────────────────────

SEMANTIC RESEARCH

Analyze $ SUBJECT and infer:

SUBJECT_TYPE =
    city
    place
    historical event
    decade / era
    cultural movement
    invention
    scientific event
    person
    sport
    country
    institution
    technology
    franchise
    abstract topic
    other

TITLE = shortest instantly recognizable name for $ SUBJECT

HERO =
choose the strongest central character or personification.

HERO may be:
    a person
    explorer
    historical figure
    citizen
    mascot
    profession
    archetype
    invented representative character

Do NOT force a person if the subject is better represented by
an object, machine, animal, landmark, or symbolic figure.

ICON_SET = select 8–16 highly recognizable subject-specific elements.

Possible classes:

    landmarks
    buildings
    transportation
    foods
    tools
    inventions
    animals
    clothing
    products
    documents
    symbols
    flags
    signs
    machines
    technologies
    landscapes
    historical artifacts
    cultural objects
    entertainment objects

SCENE_SET = infer 2–5 important environments or moments.

TEXT_SNIPPETS = infer only a few short useful labels such as:

    dates
    locations
    transit names
    famous phrases
    event names
    eras
    institutions

Never turn the poster into an infographic.

────────────────────────────────

CENTRAL CHARACTER SYSTEM

Create one oversized friendly central character.

Visual anatomy:

            SYMBOL / OBJECT
       icon      icon      icon

              ◉   ◉
             CENTRAL
             CHARACTER
          ┌─────────────┐
          │ SUBJECT     │
          │ WORLD       │
          │ EMBEDDED    │
          │ INSIDE BODY │
          └─────────────┘

     object   landmark   object

             SHOES / BASE

          HUGE TITLE BELOW

The HERO occupies roughly 55–70% of the poster height.

Treat the body as a CONTAINER FOR THE SUBJECT.

Examples:

city →
cityscape forms torso or clothing

historical event →
event scene spreads across suit/body

decade →
fashion, technology and entertainment occupy clothing and surroundings

science →
equipment, diagrams and discoveries populate body

country →
landmarks, foods, wildlife and culture become costume

invention →
components and consequences become surrounding characters

────────────────────────────────

ANTHROPOMORPHIC PROP RULE

Give selected secondary objects:

    oversized googly eyes
    tiny curved smiles
    simplified limbs only when useful

Examples:

taxi
pizza
planet
flag
camera
cassette
robot
rocket
building
food
tool

may become friendly miniature characters.

Do NOT anthropomorphize everything.

Approximately 30–50% of important props may have faces.

This creates the playful children's-editorial feeling.

────────────────────────────────

COMPOSITION

Use a dense vertical pyramid composition.

TOP:
small floating icons / symbols

UPPER CENTER:
large hero face

MIDSECTION:
largest concentration of landmarks,
objects and subject-specific scenes

LOWER SECTION:
transportation / food / secondary objects /
ground-level details

BOTTOM:
massive subject title

Use overlapping scale changes aggressively.

Objects may float beside the hero.

Buildings may emerge directly from clothing.

Vehicles may drive across the torso.

Landmarks may sit behind the head.

Objects may extend beyond the body silhouette.

The composition should feel like one enormous
illustrated sticker collage, NOT separate panels.

────────────────────────────────

STYLE

playful mid-century children's editorial illustration
× contemporary paper-cut collage
× 1960s educational poster
× kawaii object character design
× bold retro souvenir graphics

Use:

flat vector-like shapes
cut-paper construction
slightly imperfect handmade geometry
simple rounded characters
large circular eyes
tiny smiling mouths
minimal noses
primitive geometric anatomy
friendly disproportion
thick simplified silhouettes
subtle printed-paper grain
soft screenprint texture
very restrained shading
clean crisp edges
occasional paper overlap
slight tactile depth

Avoid:

Multi-objective protein optimization via modular diffusion steering

1 MODS is a modular framework that turns multi-objective protein design into inference-time steering of a fixed pretrained diffusion model, aiming to recover diverse Pareto tradeoffs under tight experimental-style budgets (few batched rounds).

2 Key idea: for each candidate proposal, MODS samples (a) augmented Chebyshev scalarization weights and (b) one member from a surrogate ensemble, combining them into a single scalar reward used for steering. Weight sampling explores different objective preferences; ensemble-member sampling explores predictive uncertainty.

3 The scalarization uses an augmented Chebyshev form: it emphasizes improving the worst-performing (weighted) objective while still rewarding progress on the others, helping recover tradeoffs on non-convex Pareto fronts where simple weighted sums can fail.

4 MODS separates “what to optimize” (multi-objective acquisition via scalar rewards) from “how to generate” (diffusion model + steering method). This makes the approach plug-and-play with different diffusion priors and compatible steering procedures.

5 Optimization loop: start with an initial evaluated set (100 sequences), then iterate 8 rounds of batched acquisition (100 sequences/round). After each round, MODS retrains only the fitness surrogate ensemble on accumulated observations, and reuses the same pretrained diffusion generator (no generator fine-tuning).

6 Implementations tested: two diffusion priors (MDLM masked diffusion LM; D3PM discrete diffusion) and two steering procedures (Classifier Guidance, CG; Decoupled Annealing Posterior Sampling, DAPS). Main comparisons focus on DAPS because it performed best across tasks.

7 Evaluation spans six assay-derived oracle benchmarks (5 two-objective tasks: GB1, ERBIN-PDZ1, NHERF3-PDZ2, KRAS, Src; 1 three-objective task: NHERF3-PDZ1). Oracles are CNN ensembles trained on experimental assay datasets with a distance-based penalty to discourage overconfident extrapolation far from labeled mutational neighborhoods.

8 Results: across all tasks, MODS improves substantially over unsteered sampling from the same diffusion model, and is competitive or best versus iterative baselines (ARLM+DPO, LaMBO-2, SAGE-Prot). In Table 1, MODS achieves the top mean final hypervolume on 5/6 tasks with D3PM+DAPS, and is close to the best baseline on Src with MDLM+DAPS.

9 Practical insight: steering strength matters. Too-weak regularization (oversteering away from the diffusion prior) can hurt on some tasks, consistent with reliance on less reliable surrogate predictions; the optimal setting depends jointly on task, diffusion prior, and steering procedure.

How much should a robot policy trust each simulated demonstration when only a few real ones exist? BEACON, a NeurIPS 2026 paper from @hankyang94's group at Harvard with Brown, learns this instead of fixing a sim-to-real mixing ratio.

It trains a Diffusion Policy together with a weight for each simulated training sample. The weights come from a domain-adaptation bound (Best-Effort Adaptation): a sample that sits far from the real data gets less say in training.

On a Franka arm with 500 simulated and 40 real demonstrations, a sim-only policy scores 0 and a real-only one 0.08. BEACON reaches an average real-robot score of 0.79, against 0.62 for the best baseline, and 0.83 with two simulated sources.

The surprising part: closer feature alignment does not mean better transfer. When objects start outside the demonstrated region, stacking with the alignment baseline MMD falls from 0.40 to 0.05, while BEACON keeps 0.35.

A recent post on DiscoDemo (https://t.co/z0ltBGBiU4) covered generating extra demonstrations with RL; BEACON is about how much each such demonstration should count. Work led by Antong Zhang and Han Qi. Paper: https://t.co/ZmpHgjTcuq
